analysisDescription: From what I remembered and looked online, I visualized what I thought was right.

dimensionExamples.example: Players can unlock crafting recipes or raft upgrades, these unlockables are shared because they are like an item.

dimension.title: Unlockables
dimension.description: Unlockables refer to content available in the gameplay but not accessible up until players are able and choose to get access to it. Usually, games limit the number of unlocks a player can acquire. Unlockables are shared when the decision to unlock new content pertains to more than one player. The effect of the unlockables may or may not be shared (it might affect only one player, but they would still be shared if more than one player could make the decision).

dimensionExamples.example: Interactables include items such as fishing rods and cooking pots. One player can cook while another fishes, both using the raft’s resources together.

dimension.title: Interactables
dimension.description: Interactables refer to virtual objects and non-player characters/entities within the environment that respond to players’ actions. Interactables can be moved, shaped, or activated (e.g., a cannon that shoots when the player interacts with it). In some cases, interactables are also consumable (e.g., food in Overcooked is transported and modified as an interactable, but also consumed to complete the recipes). Interactables are shared when their state and attributes can be affected by more than one player.

dimensionExamples.example: One player begins the save and can play alone or with others and join or leave whenever they want.

dimension.title: Drop-in/Drop-out
dimension.description: Drop-in/Drop-out encompasses games where there is the ability for players to join in the midst of the gameplay and drop out at any point.

dimensionExamples.example: All players work together to gather resources, build a raft, and navigate in the sea. The team’s success depends on shared efforts in resource management and decision-making.

dimension.title: Shared
dimension.description: Shared goals consist of singular objectives that multiple players pursue and work together to achieve

dimensionExamples.example: Players are a group of survivors on a raft that travels along the sea. They explore and do everything in the game together.

dimension.title: Party
dimension.description: Party progression results from the contributions of a group of players that opted to play together, where part of the progress is solely associated with that group (not shared with the rest of the server or community).

dimensionExamples.example: Each player controls one single survivor, never switching to another one.

dimension.title: Single
dimension.description: Single applies to any game where players have control of one single entity.

dimensionExamples.example: Each player has full control of their character

dimension.title: Distinct
dimension.description: Distinct means that each player controls a different entity or set of entities

dimensionExamples.example: Players start with the skin that they choose in the first menu and it is merely an aesthetic choice.

dimension.title: Arbitrary
dimension.description: Arbitrary means that all player entities are equal in their ability to act upon the world. If a selection exists, it is merely an aesthetic choice.

dimensionExamples.example: There is no progression in the game, so the player entities do not change throughout the gameplay.

dimension.title: Static
dimension.description: When the player's entity is constant throughout gameplay.

dimensionExamples.example: Players must coordinate their roles to achieve a common goal. One person steers the raft, another looks for islands, someone gathers resources, and another defends the boat from the shark.

dimension.title: Teammates
dimension.description: Teammates, where players within a team need to coordinate their actions, abilities, and roles in order to reach a common goal against at least another team.

dimensionExamples.example: All players share the same world.

dimension.title: Shared
dimension.description: Shared world views apply to a game when players have access to the same world.

dimensionExamples.example: Each player has their own unique perspective and does not share screens or views with others.

dimension.title: Distinct
dimension.description: Distinct refers to when each player has control of their own individual viewpoint, typically through separate screens.

dimensionExamples.example: Players can gather resources, fish, build, or manage the raft without predefined roles.

dimension.title: Free Collaboration
dimension.description: In free collaboration, players can take on available tasks as they wish and decide how to contribute.

dimensionExamples.example: One player needs to steer the raft while another collects resources from the sea.

dimension.title: Coupled Collaboration
dimension.description: In coupled collaboration, players take on different tasks that somehow intertwine and typically contribute to a shared outcome.

dimensionExamples.example: All players can collect resources from the sea.

dimension.title: Coincident Collaboration
dimension.description: In coincident collaboration, players are accomplishing the same task together.

dimensionExamples.example: Players are expected to coordinate their actions and work together in real time. For example: steer the raft and defending against the shark.

dimension.title: Concurrent Collaboration
dimension.description: In concurrent collaboration, players have to perform gameplay tasks concurrently.

dimensionExamples.example: Players can collaborate effectively without constant communication. However, coordinating actions such as gathering resources and defending the raft benefits the team, though it is not strictly required by the game’s mechanics.

dimension.title: Agnostic
dimension.description: When Agnostic, the game is neutral to player communication, it does not incentivise nor it places any restrictions. It is the only communication design that does not promote cooperation.

dimensionExamples.example: The game includes an in-game text chat where players can send messages to one another.

dimension.title: Text Chat
dimension.description: Support for players to communicate using text

dimensionExamples.example: Players might shoot their bows or drop items like resources on the ground to signal that others should pick them up or use them. Normal stuff.

dimension.title: In-Game Movement/Actions
dimension.description: Players can communicate through specific movement or actions (e.g. shooting a weapon on the ground to notify others to pick it up)

dimensionExamples.example: To craft a bow, you first need to gather resources. Tasks such as crafting and defending against sharks often require coordinated efforts.

dimension.title: Task
dimension.description: Task refers to gameplay tasks where at least one player is dependent on another. These can force players to coordinate to be effective and complete them.

dimensionExamples.example: Players who venture too far from the raft risk shark attacks, which incentivizes staying close to each other and raft.

dimension.title: Spatial
dimension.description: Spatial, inspired by Reuter et al. 2014, happens when the game forces or incentivises players to be at a certain distance from one another. This can happen in a variety of ways, for example, by creating a radius around which players cannot trespass or by designing mechanics that punish players that move too far away from the group.

dimensionExamples.example: When a player dies from a shark attack or from hunger, you can revive them, which increases your chance of survival.

dimension.title: Assistive Actions
dimension.description: Assistive Actions encompass actions that one player performs to the benefit of other/s (i.e. note that the player can have indirect benefits such as reviving others to increase their own chances of success). In these games, players can support and assist other players in achieving their objectives.

dimensionExamples.example: Food and fresh water are essential for survival; they prevent you from dying.

dimension.title: Consumables
dimension.description: Consumables refer to items that exist in a limited amount and can be utilised by players to invoke an effect (usually existing as a form of currency, materials, or food) or are not consumed on purpose by players but support the gameplay (e.g., health, energy). Consumables are shared when the agency to consume and manage them pertains to more than one player.

dimensionExamples.example: One player spots an island in the distance while the others work on the raft. He can communicate this information to help the group decide what to do next.

dimension.title: Information
dimension.description: Information, as described by Harris et al. 2016, is where one player knows something other players do not. In cooperative games, this is leveraged by ensuring the information is needed to be shared, or acted upon by more than the player with access to the knowledge. This is typically instantiated with players having Distinct - Player Views and Worlds.

dimensionExamples.example: In the game, there are no official roles assigned; however, players naturally take on different responsibilities, such as steering the raft, gathering resources, defending against the shark, and expanding the raft. This informal division of roles helps players cover each other's weaknesses, ensuring that the team is well-rounded and capable of responding effectively to the various challenges they encounter.

dimension.title: Complementarity
dimension.description: Complementarity, extended from Rocha et. al rocha2008game, corresponds to when player actions are designed to balance each other’s weaknesses or so that strengths complement each other. It is typically achieved through asymmetric game design, with each player bringing something to the shared experience.
